For Staff - Intermediate
STAFF REFERENCE
What a skill actually is

1A packaged, reusable capability

A skill is a reusable capability packaged in a file (a SKILL.md, plus optional scripts and reference files) that teaches Claude how to do one specific job a consistent way.

2It loads progressively

Only the skill's name and a short description sit in Claude's context until your request matches it, then the full instructions load. That keeps things fast, and it means you can have many skills available without slowing Claude down.

3It's portable

The same skill file works across Claude.ai, Cowork, Claude Code, and the API. It's an open format, not a one-off.

4It comes from a few places

Built-in ones from Anthropic (docx, pptx, xlsx, pdf), custom ones uploaded to our School Tech org, and personal ones an individual installs.

How you use them

You don't trigger a skill by hand. Claude reads your request and auto-runs the matching skill. You just ask naturally.

Example: "write this up as a help article" fires the Help Center Article skill; "make this a checklist" fires the HTML Checklist skill. You never type a command.

  • Built-in skills (Word, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF) are always available.
  • Our STA custom skills are uploaded to the org, so they're available in the right tools.
  • In Cowork you install a skill from its file; in a Claude.ai Project, skills activate automatically when relevant (some need code execution turned on).
Nothing to memorize: if a skill exists for your task, describing the task is enough.
The skills we've built

We have a growing set of STA custom skills - help-article writing, checklists, the prompt-override guard, time-clock log review, and the build-pipeline tools.

See the full list: the AI Admin tab has every one of our custom skills and what each does.
When to make a new one
The question is whether a behavior should be its own skill or just live in a project's instructions.
Make a skill when
It's a repeatable procedure
It's only needed some of the time
It has a clear start and a clear output
It's long (roughly 200+ lines of steps)
Document-creation patterns, audits, and workflows fit here.
Keep it inline when
It defines who the agent is
It's a hard rule the agent must follow every time
It's the tone the agent always uses
Identity and always-on rules belong in the project's instructions.
Quick heuristic: facts and identity go in the instructions; repeatable procedures become a skill.
What makes a skill work
The description is the most important part. It's what tells Claude when to fire the skill, so it has to name the real phrases people say and the artifacts involved.

Two ways a skill misfires, and both trace back to a weak description:

  • Undertriggering - it never fires when it should.
  • Overtriggering - it fires when it shouldn't.

At School Tech we build skills through the skill-creator tool, which enforces the description quality, the length limit, and runs an eval loop before a skill ships. That's why our skills trigger reliably.
